newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa confident of partial accession to Lome.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa confident of partial accession to Lome.

text.p: South Africa is confident of gaining partial membership of the Lome Convention, smoothing the way for a free trade deal with the European Union, Trade and Industry Minister Alec Erwin said.

The EU and Pretoria said after hard bargaining at the weekend that they were moving closer to agreement on a free trade deal, including access to Lome, which grants favourable access to EU markets to 70 developing countries elsewhere in Africa, the Caribbean and Pacific (ACP).
Erwin told Reuters that South Africa had previously received assurances from the ACP block of access to Lome.
"We are pretty confident that that should be possible soon," he said in an interview late on Tuesday.
Referring to talks on a future free trade deal with the EU, Erwin said: "One should understand that the process depends as much on the ACP countries as it does on the European Union".

The EU -- under pressure from its own farming lobby -- has refused post-apartheid South Africa full accession to Lome. Nearly 40 percent of South African agricultural exports would be excluded under initial EU proposals.
Other outstanding issues on Pretoria's entry into Lome include South African companies' participation in European Development Fund contracts in Africa.
Erwin said one of the major benefits of access to Lome, even if it was only partial, was preferential tariffs on goods.

"The other issue that we are looking at is in the ACP system: the products of one ACP member that are sold to another would qualify as so-called local content for that country's onward sale to the European Union.

"We are particularly interested in that because of the synergy it would create in southern Africa and given our very rapidly expanding favourable trade balance with our Southern African Development Community (SADC) partners."
Erwin said this would provide a genuine benefit to South Africa's neighbours by giving access to the EU market more effectively.

There have been growing concerns within the southern Africa region and the 12-member SADC about the impact of a free trade deal between Pretoria and Brussels on the economies of some of South Africa's smaller neighbours.
But Erwin said both negotiating teams indicated that the interests of SADC should come before that of the European Union.
"As both negotiating teams indicated, the principle of SADC coming before the EU...should proceed.
"We indicated and it was made clear that we saw SADC's position as being crucial and within that concern the EU negotiations would be accommodated," he said.

The next round of talks would be held in Brussels next month and South Africa hopes the ACP/EU Council of Ministers will be able to approve terms and conditions of access to Lome at its meeting on April 24 and 25 in Luxembourg.
The current trade talks come in the wake of South Africa outlining its negotiating position on a trade deal with the EU last month in response to Brussels' mandate which was presented in March 1996.
The EU has accused Pretoria of dragging its feet while South African parliamentarians initially lambasted the EU's proposal to exclude much of South Africa's agricultural produce from a future deal.
